record.title: Graph-guided red-teaming finds more harmful cross-service paths in a simulated personal-agent ecosystem
record.summary: The October 2026 X-AgentRed preprint uses a graph of tool effects and execution preconditions to generate cross-service red-team scenarios, then uses execution feedback to diversify successful paths and repair blocked ones. In one evaluation run per configuration across four target agents in a simulated ecosystem of 30 services and 914 tools, the authors report a 19.2% harmful-path rate, versus 10.5% for STAC and 2.7% for TRACE; average tool coverage is 41.5%, versus 13.9% and 23.7%. These are paper-reported simulator results, not estimates of real-world agent risk.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: X-AgentRed builds a directed graph connecting tool effects to other tools' execution preconditions, samples cross-service paths from this HarmFlow graph, and uses execution feedback to diversify paths that produce harm and refine blocked paths.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In a simulated ecosystem with 30 services and 914 tools, the authors report average harmful-path rates of 19.2% for X-AgentRed, 10.5% for STAC, and 2.7% for TRACE across four target agents, using 250 candidate scenarios per target.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report average tool coverage of 41.5% for X-AgentRed, compared with 13.9% for STAC and 23.7% for TRACE. Each configuration was evaluated in one run in the fixed simulator; judge aggregation materially changes the reported harmful-path rate.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The arXiv record identifies version 1 and submission at 2026-10-09 17:34 UTC. This verifies the preprint and its date, not independent validation of its results.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction of the one-run-per-configuration results or judge labels was examined.
The reported environment is simulated; transfer to changing real service integrations and deployed-agent safeguards is unknown.

brief.importance_rationale: If the paper's reported result generalizes beyond the single-run simulated ecosystem, graph-guided exploration could materially improve discovery of unintended harms in personal agents that combine services. The evidence is a controlled benchmark result reported by the authors, not field prevalence or production-agent risk.
limitations: Each configuration was evaluated in one run, so run-to-run variability is not estimated.
The testbed is a simulated ecosystem, not deployed agents connected to production services; the results do not establish field prevalence or production risk.

The main harmful-path rate requires agreement by two model judges. Accepting either judge raises rates by 15.2–30.4 percentage points relative to agreement, and the paper says this measures sensitivity rather than judge accuracy.
The longer executed workflows and differing baseline path statistics complicate interpretation of coverage and harmful-path comparisons.
No independent reproduction or artifact inspection was performed in this review.
brief.summary: The October 2026 X-AgentRed preprint uses a graph of tool effects and execution preconditions to generate cross-service red-team scenarios, then uses execution feedback to diversify successful paths and repair blocked ones. In one evaluation run per configuration across four target agents in a simulated ecosystem of 30 services and 914 tools, the authors report a 19.2% harmful-path rate, versus 10.5% for STAC and 2.7% for TRACE; average tool coverage is 41.5%, versus 13.9% and 23.7%. These are paper-reported simulator results, not estimates of real-world agent risk.

technical.claimed_result: Authors report mean harmful-path rates of 19.2% for X-AgentRed, 10.5% for STAC and 2.7% for TRACE, and mean tool coverage of 41.5%, 13.9% and 23.7%, respectively.
technical.demonstrated_result: The arXiv v1 full text, experiment protocol, reported results and limitations were inspected. No independent reproduction was performed.
technical.implementation_status: The preprint describes the method and simulated experiments. No code was executed and no independent replication or deployed-service evaluation was performed.
technical.mechanism: The system represents each tool by execution preconditions, effects and possible harms. A language model assesses effect–precondition links to form the HarmFlow dependency graph; graph walks generate candidate recipes. Executed scenarios are diversified through adjacent tool substitutions after success, while blocked paths are refined by adjusting preconditions and preceding steps.
technical.novelty: Combines an explicit cross-tool dependency graph with execution-guided diversification and repair to search compositions across a simulated service ecosystem.
technical.regime: Author evaluation using ToolSimulator with 30 services and 914 tools; four target agent models; 250 scenarios per target; one run per configuration. Two model judges must agree for the main harmful-path labels.
technical.reproducibility: The paper's reported evaluation was inspected in the HTML. One run per configuration limits uncertainty estimation; no independent run or external simulator audit was performed. The arXiv-linked project page was not inspected for executable artifacts.
technical.strongest_baseline: STAC is the strongest reported baseline on mean harmful-path rate (10.5%) and TRACE covers more tools on average than STAC (23.7% versus 13.9%); X-AgentRed reports 19.2% HPR and 41.5% coverage. Comparisons come from one run per configuration in the authors' fixed simulator.

brief.title: Graph-guided red-teaming finds more harmful cross-service paths in a simulated personal-agent ecosystem
brief.why_it_matters: A dependency graph can expose combinations of individually benign tool actions that prompt-based red-teaming may miss. The reported benchmark advantage makes this a notable testing method for service-using agents, while a single simulated run and judge-sensitive labels leave its field relevance uncertain.
